title: Splitting Components — When and Where to Break Things Apart

subChunks.title: Splitting Components — When and Where to Break Things Apart
subChunks.hookHtml: Every beginner writes components that are too big. Every intermediate developer splits too eagerly and ends up with a forest of tiny files nobody can navigate. The skill is knowing the right time to extract a component — and doing it decisively when that time comes. This isn't art; there are concrete signals that tell you when a component has grown past its natural boundary.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The signals that say 'extract this'

Extract a component when any one of these is true:

  1. You're repeating the same JSX structure with minor variations — that's a component waiting to be written
  2. A section of a component needs its own state that the parent doesn't care about
  3. You can name it — if you can say "this section is a UserCard" or "this is the EmptyState", it should be a component
  4. The component is too tall to read without scrolling — if you can't see the return statement and the state together, consider splitting
  5. Two different pages need the same UI pattern — extract before you copy-paste

The signals that say 'not yet'

  • The section only appears once and has no name that would be meaningful
  • The section's logic is tightly tangled with the parent's state
  • Extracting would require drilling three or more props down just to connect it back

Vex: "A component that takes 12 props to work is a component that extracted too early. It's still a piece of the parent — it just has a name now. That's not composition; that's a function with extra steps."

Where to put extracted components

There are three natural homes for a component you extract:

  1. Same file — for small helper components used only by one parent. Keep them in the same file, below the main export. Don't create a file for everything.
  2. Sibling file — when the component grows enough to deserve its own file, create UserCard.jsx next to the file that uses it.
  3. Shared components folder — when used in two or more places, promote it to components/ or shared/.
// ✅ Small helper — same file is fine
function QuestBadge({ tier }) {
  return <span className={`badge badge-${tier}`}>{tier}</span>;
}

export default function QuestList({ quests }) {
  return (
    <ul>
      {quests.map(q => (
        <li key={q.id}>
          {q.title}
          <QuestBadge tier={q.tier} />  {/* same file — no import needed */}
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}

The rule of three for promotion

When a component appears in a third location, promote it to shared. First use: inline. Second use: extract to its own file. Third use: move to components/. This avoids over-engineering early and under-engineering late.

Practical example — before and after

// ❌ Before — one monolith, hard to navigate:
export default function Dashboard() {
  const [user, setUser] = useState(null);
  const [quests, setQuests] = useState([]);
  const [notifications, setNotifications] = useState([]);
  // ...80 more lines...
  return (
    <div>
      <header>
        <img src={user.avatar} />
        <span>{user.name}</span>
        <span>{user.xp} XP</span>
      </header>
      <section>
        {quests.map(q => (<div key={q.id}>...long quest row...</div>))}
      </section>
      <aside>
        {notifications.map(n => (<div key={n.id}>...notification...</div>))}
      </aside>
    </div>
  );
}

// ✅ After — same file, three focused components:
function UserHeader({ user }) {
  return (
    <header>
      <img src={user.avatar} />
      <span>{user.name}</span>
      <span>{user.xp} XP</span>
    </header>
  );
}

function QuestRow({ quest }) {
  return <div>...focused quest row...</div>;
}

function NotificationItem({ notification }) {
  return <div>...notification...</div>;
}

export default function Dashboard() {
  const [user, setUser] = useState(null);
  const [quests, setQuests] = useState([]);
  const [notifications, setNotifications] = useState([]);
  return (
    <div>
      <UserHeader user={user} />
      <section>{quests.map(q => <QuestRow key={q.id} quest={q} />)}</section>
      <aside>{notifications.map(n => <NotificationItem key={n.id} notification={n} />)}</aside>
    </div>
  );
}

storyBeats.text: Vex unfurls a blueprint on the table — a tower floor plan. At first it's one undivided room. She draws walls, creating a bedroom, a library, a laboratory. 'The space is the same,' she says. 'But now each room has a purpose. You know where to find things.'

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: Don't extract components to feel organised. Extract them because a section has a name, because it repeats, because it needs its own state that the parent doesn't care about. Those are real reasons. 'It feels big' is not.

storyBeats.speaker: Rule of three for promotion

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
You are given a single UserProfile component that renders an avatar, a stats section, and a list of recent quests. Extract two helper components in the same file:

  • UserAvatar — renders <img data-testid="avatar" src={src} alt={name} />
  • QuestItem — renders <li data-testid="quest-item">{title}</li>

The UserProfile default export should use these helpers.

guidedPracticeTests.label: Renders correct number of quest items

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a <ProductGrid> from scratch. It renders a grid of products from a hardcoded array. Extract at minimum: a ProductCard component (renders image, name, price) and an EmptyState component (shown when the array is empty). Both should live in the same file as ProductGrid. Add a 'Clear' button that empties the product array to test the empty state.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a junior developer the three signals that tell you it's time to extract a component — and the three signals that tell you not to yet. Give a concrete example of over-splitting (extracting too eagerly) and explain the harm it causes.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest signal that a section of JSX should be extracted into its own component?
options: The same JSX structure appears in more than one place with minor variations
The section is more than 10 lines of JSX
The section has more than 2 HTML elements
The developer wants to give the section a descriptive name
questions.answer: The same JSX structure appears in more than one place with minor variations
questions.explanation: Repetition is the strongest signal — duplicated JSX structure means you'll need to update it in multiple places when requirements change. Length and element count are weak signals; a 15-line section that only appears once and has no natural name may be fine inline. Wanting a name is a positive signal but weaker than actual repetition.

questions.prompt: A helper component is used in exactly two places in the same feature folder. Where should it live?
options: Its own file in the same feature folder, imported by both parents
In the global components/ folder immediately
Duplicated inline in both parents to avoid coupling
In a separate package published to npm
questions.answer: Its own file in the same feature folder, imported by both parents
questions.explanation: At two uses, extract to its own file close to where it's used. The global components/ folder is for components used across features — promoting too early adds noise to shared space. Duplication is never the right answer for UI components. npm is for code shared between projects.

questions.prompt: A component takes 9 props. What does this most likely indicate?
options: It was extracted too early — it may still be a conceptual part of its parent and the split should be reconsidered
It is a well-designed component with a clear, comprehensive interface
It needs to be split into 9 individual single-prop components
Props should be replaced with a React context to reduce the count
questions.answer: It was extracted too early — it may still be a conceptual part of its parent and the split should be reconsidered
questions.explanation: A large prop count is a code smell suggesting the component is not truly independent — it's just the parent's logic wearing a different name. The fix may be to merge it back, to pass a single object prop (grouping related values), or to redesign the abstraction. Context solves prop drilling across many levels, but it doesn't fix poorly designed component boundaries.
